state: Three workloads were each written three ways, giving nine complete Can sources. The file workload streams a large JSONL input and stops at the first record whose typed id satisfies the predicate. The process workload consumes merged stdout/stderr text chunks into grouped byte counts, honors a cancellation budget, then reaps and enforces the exit. The socket workload serves one accepted session, tallying text messages and binary bytes, observing drain and close, and halting on protocol failure. The library surface routes all three through one generic stream::consume call: native code loops, invokes the named handler per item, and interprets continue/stop decisions. The per-domain surface duplicates that loop per module, so files::lines, process::drain_output and socket::serve each define their own options, decision nominals and failures. The shared-event surface publishes opaque stream::reader<T>/stream::writer values with read_many, write_some, close and cancel; callers recurse, an empty batch terminates normally, and each terminal path closes handles and re-raises the primary failure by reconstruction. Today's grammar accepts every one of the nine files, and canlc assert faults only the invented catalogue pieces: the stream and socket packages, plus decision nominals such as files::line_decision. Proven building blocks: $callback checking with derived handler errors ships in array.fold; decision-shaped callbacks ship in sql::with_transaction; self-recursion without annotations runs; withFixture narrows rows to the running assertion and replays them in FIFO order under per-visit identities, flagging surplus reads as missing fixture and surplus rows as unused fixture; the engine furnishes opaque givens that when rows may cite; failure patterns bind payloads (as failed) and arms rebuild them.
